header:
Date: 2026-12-09
Start: 16:00 PT
Duration: 47 minutes
Recording: yes
Attendees: Alex Morgan (Redwood AE); Priya Shah (Redwood SE); Marcus Li (Redwood Solutions); Evan Lee (CTO, Opaline); Sara Morales (Sr ML Engineer); Jordan Park (Platform Eng); Maya Ortiz (Security)
summary: Initial migration discovery and sprint kickoff. Customer currently on Anthropic + vLLM self-host for part of traffic, some calls to OpenAI. Main drivers: cost predictability, SLA for peak trading hours, data residency for EMEA, and private deployment options. Discussed compatibility concerns (TGI/vLLM artifacts, tokenizer differences), quantization, KV cache behavior, streaming parity, and security (SOC2, KMS, SSO). Agreed pilot: Redwood to run parity benchmarks against Opaline's prompt sets on hosted/Dedicated and provide a runbook; Opaline to provide prompts, outputs, and infra constraints.
transcript:
[00:00] Alex Morgan: Hey everyone, thanks for taking time. quick check — can you hear me okay?
[00:03] Evan Lee: Yeah, loud and clear, thanks Alex.
[00:07] Priya Shah: Hi — Priya here from Redwood, I'll cover the technical bits.
[00:11] Sara Morales: Sara from Opaline. We're excited to kick this off — we've been talking about moving some workloads off our self-hosted vLLM fleet.
[00:18] Alex Morgan: Cool. quick agenda: status, constraints, what parity means for you, and then pilot plan. Evan do you want to frame why you're looking?
[00:29] Evan Lee: Sure. So high level: we have a mixed stack. currently running Anthropic Claude via managed service for chat, some finetuned endpoints on OpenAI, and for scale experiments we self-host vLLM on GCP. The thing is — costs are ballooning and reliability during our peak window is concern, also compliance — EMEA data must remain in our VPC.
[00:52] Jordan Park: to add, our ops team spends too much time on kernel tuning and instance churn.
[00:57] Alex Morgan: Makes sense. Priya — any immediate compatibility gotchas you anticipate?
[01:03] Priya Shah: yeah couple. vLLM exports and TGI checkpoints can be mostly compatible but tokenizer variants and special tokens sometimes change outputs. also kv cache semantics — how the runtime manages incremental state — that affects latency for multi-turn chat. we want to validate output parity not byte-for-byte but behavioral parity.
[01:26] Sara Morales: when you say behavioral parity, give an example? like does priority go to identical responses? or same safety class?
[01:33] Priya Shah: good question. For us parity often means same answer intent and key facts preserved, same hallucination rate within threshold, and comparable latency/throughput. so we'll run three families of tests: intent/classification, long-form summarization, and agent-style step-by-step reasoning.
[01:49] Evan Lee: ok that aligns. our SLOs: p95 latency for chat under 350ms for 8k contexts ideally, throughput of ~250 reqs/min sustained on peaks. cost target is 40% reduction vs self-hosted vLLM TCO.
[02:08] Marcus Li: quick clarifier — are those numbers for inference on your current quantized models?
[02:12] Jordan Park: yes, we run int8 quant on several models and some bf16 on bigger experiments.
[02:18] Priya Shah: good to note. quantization differences between our runtime and their self-hosted stack can lead to tiny quality shifts — we'll flag that and suggest quant profiles.
[02:28] Maya Ortiz: security: we need end-to-end encryption of keys, KMS integration that supports our HSMs, SSO for the control plane with SAML, and audit logs forwarded to our SIEM. SOC2 is mandatory. any red flags?
[02:42] Alex Morgan: Redwood supports SSO/SAML and KMS integrations; for Private we can integrate with customer-managed KMS/HSM. we have SOC2 Type II and can provide the report. audit logs are available and can be shipped; we'll share docs.
[02:56] Evan Lee: EMEA residency — we need logs and any model inputs to stay in our EU VPC for certain widths of data. can Redwood guarantee that?
[03:05] Priya Shah: on Private yes. for Dedicated we can set region pinning and for Hosted we have EU regions but additional contractual clauses might be needed. we'll note that for the runbook.
[03:16] Sara Morales: technical deep dive: how do you handle model variants? we use TGI for serving some finetuned variants with custom tokenizers. will that move easily?
[03:27] Priya Shah: often yes — we accept TGI-style checkpoints, but there are a few steps: ensure tokenizer metadata is preserved (tokenizer.json), confirm config flags like use_fast_tokenizer, and map any custom ops. sometimes small adapter scripts needed. we'll propose a migration checklist.
[03:43] Alex Morgan: perfect. Evan — what does success look like for the pilot?
[03:47] Evan Lee: two parts: 1) functional parity on our canonical prompts (we'll provide three sets), and 2) operational: an infra plan for either Dedicated or Private with cost estimates and SLA. ideally we want a path to switch traffic by Q1 2027.
[04:03] Priya Shah: timeline sounds doable. for parity we recommend a 2-week sprint: week 1 baseline runs on Redwood hosted and dedicated, week 2 root cause for any diffs and apply tuning/quant profiles.
[04:15] Jordan Park: curious about canary routing — if we run hybrid do you support split routing between Dedicated and Hosted?
[04:22] Marcus Li: yes, Redwood supports smart routing by policy. you can route by latency, region, cost, or customer tier. also fallback to smaller variants if a model is unavailable.
[04:34] Sara Morales: mention of fallback — in our internal experiments fallback slightly changes conversation flow which is fine but we need deterministic behavior for audits. how deterministic are fallbacks?
[04:44] Priya Shah: we can make routing deterministic for a route id and provide consistent hashing to keep sessions stable. we'll include session affinity options in the runbook.
[04:53] Evan Lee: logs — need to be able to tie token usage back to request ids for billing reconciliation.
[04:58] Alex Morgan: that's part of the Console features — token-level cost breakdowns and per-route dashboards, and we can add a trace id to each request.
[05:07] [05:07] Speaker 2 (transcript artifact): uh yeah can you repeat the storage retention details?
[05:09] Maya Ortiz: we want short-term storage of raw prompts denied for compliance for anything PII, but retain fingerprints and audit trails for 1 year.
[05:18] Priya Shah: we support configurable retention. for Private the customer controls retention. for Hosted we have redact/retention configs and can do prompt hashing. we'll surface the options.
[05:28] Sara Morales: down to nitty gritty — when you do KV cache and prefix cache, does Redwood share KV cache across models or it's per-model instance?
[05:36] Priya Shah: per-model and per-deployment, but we can cache prefixes across similar model variants with correct keying; we'd need to instrument session keys properly. this can reduce token cost significantly for repeated prompts.
[05:47] Evan Lee: want to touch on streaming and function calls: we use streaming extensively; some of our orchestration assumes chunked streaming semantics similar to OpenAI. any differences?
[05:58] Priya Shah: our hosted API supports streaming with chunk semantics and server-sent events. function-calling patterns are supported; caveat is that sometimes tokenization boundary differences can shift chunk boundaries. we'll test with your orchestrator.
[06:11] Jordan Park: our ops want to run a bench: can Redwood run our test harness or do we run against your endpoints?
[06:17] Alex Morgan: both options. for quick parity we can run the Redwood-run bench with your datasets (preferred for consistency). we'll provide the harness and collaborate on runs.
[06:26] Evan Lee: Ok. I also want to understand Dedicated vs Private tradeoffs — cost delta, ops overhead.
[06:32] Marcus Li: Dedicated is Redwood-managed reserved pools; you get predictable throughput, data isolation at the tenant level, and SLA. Private runs the control plane in your VPC or fully on-prem — more control, more integration work, and typically higher fixed cost. We'll provide rough numbers.
[06:47] Sara Morales: and hardware — do you support A40s / H100s and automatic kernel selection? we need to know quantization support per GPU type.
[06:55] Priya Shah: yes H100 and A100 families supported; runtime selects kernels based on model arch and sequence length. quantization profiles differ; we'll recommend a profile that matches your current int8 results.
[07:06] Evan Lee: regarding cost — our finance will want a modeling spreadsheet that maps tokens to billable units across Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private.
[07:15] Alex Morgan: we'll provide a cost model. I'll include a conservative and optimistic scenario.
[07:20] [07:20] Speaker 1: brief pause —
[07:22] Maya Ortiz: any legal constraints for switching from Anthropic/OpenAI? we have some clauses about model outputs and regulatory logs.
[07:30] Alex Morgan: we can sign standard vendor transition language. for Hosted we can include data handling addendums; for Private those are easier since data never leaves your VPC.
[07:39] Priya Shah: quick technical note: if you're porting finetunes, some low level ops might be custom — we sometimes need a small adapter or re-export through TGI. it's usually mechanical.
[07:50] Sara Morales: on finetunes, we have a few adapters that change embedding dims; want to confirm Redwood supports custom head layers.
[07:58] Priya Shah: yes, with model variants you can host custom heads; we'll need weights and a repo of the inference config.
[08:05] Evan Lee: let's talk data residency — for EMEA only traffic we might want a Private control plane in EU region with Dedicated serving in EU. is that supported?
[08:15] Marcus Li: yes. route by geography and pin your models to EU Dedicated pools. control plane location for Private can be in your EU VPC.
[08:24] Jordan Park: network constraints: we have strict egress controls. for Private we'll need proxied registries and locked-down OS images.
[08:32] Priya Shah: we have an enterprise private install runbook — bootstrapped images and offline registries are supported. we'll share the slide.
[08:40] Sara Morales: anything about inference determinism — when running quantized models we sometimes see occasional nondeterministic tokens across runs. do you provide seed control?
[08:50] Priya Shah: yes you can seed the RNG for deterministic outputs in the runtime. it's config-level and we'll add it to the harness.
[08:59] Evan Lee: excellent. A few quick questions from my engineering team — 1) will you support our OpenTelemetry traces? 2) can we correlate traces with token-level costs?
[09:09] Priya Shah: yes — we have tracing hooks and can ingest OTLP; correlate request ids with token metrics in the Console.
[09:17] [09:17] Speaker 3: small chime in
[09:19] Alex Morgan: Okay, let's align on the pilot scope and deliverables. Priya, propose the parity test plan?
[09:25] Priya Shah: propose: deliverables — benchmark harness + runbook, three canonical prompt sets from Opaline, baseline run on Redwood Hosted and a short Dedicated pool, result CSVs with metrics (latency p50/p95, token counts, similarity scores), and a tuning pass. timeline: 2 weeks. success criteria: for intent tests F1 within 95% of baseline, for summarization ROUGE within delta X (we'll define), latency p95 within 20% of baseline or under target.
[09:52] Sara Morales: define delta X — we need numbers.
[09:55] Priya Shah: fair — we'll propose thresholds in the runbook: intent F1 >= 0.95, ROUGE-L within 3 points, hallucination rate within 5% absolute. open to negotiation.
[10:07] Evan Lee: that's reasonable. finance will need cost projection — Alex you'll send that.
[10:11] Alex Morgan: yep. I'll send pricing bands and pilot terms.
[10:15] Jordan Park: any tooling to automate canarying after pilot?
[10:18] Marcus Li: Console supports canary rollouts, traffic split, and automatic fallback. we also have tracing to detect regressions.
[10:26] Sara Morales: curious about how you detect quality regression automatically — do you integrate evals into the serving pipeline?
[10:33] Priya Shah: Redwood Optimize ties evaluation sets to model rollouts; we can alert on regressions against golden prompts or prompt families. we'll include that for the pilot.
[10:41] Maya Ortiz: legal will want to see the SOC2 report and an encryption spec. Alex can you share?
[10:46] Alex Morgan: yes I'll attach SOC2 Type II, encryption whitepaper, and KMS integration docs after the call.
[10:52] Evan Lee: last item — training/familiarity for our SREs; do you provide onboarding for Dedicated/Private?
[10:58] Marcus Li: yes onboarding sessions, runbook walkthroughs, and a couple of hours of SE support during pilot runs.
[11:05] Alex Morgan: great. if there's nothing else we'll recap next steps.
[11:09] Sara Morales: small question — model licensing, any restrictions on model usage or fine-tuning?
[11:15] Alex Morgan: we maintain a catalog of curated open models and Redwood-verified profiles. licensing depends on the model — if it's an open license you're fine; if it's a third-party managed model we can discuss. we'll surface model license guidance.
[11:28] Evan Lee: ok thanks. wrapping up — this was helpful.
[11:31] Alex Morgan: awesome. recap: Alex send pricing and SOC2 and pilot terms; Priya provide bench harness and runbook; Opaline to provide prompt sets and sample outputs. schedule bench run for week of Dec 20.
[11:44] Priya Shah: I'll also include a checklist for TGI/vLLM exports.
[11:48] Jordan Park: noted. thanks all.
[11:51] Maya Ortiz: thanks.
[11:53] Alex Morgan: thanks all, we'll follow up with calendar invites.
[11:56] [11:56] Speaker 2: end of recording

Notes on transcript quality: occasional speaker labeling artifacts and small words mis-transcribed; overall technical content preserved.
